B: Hi. Rana. Can you hear me?
A: Yeh, fine. Gemma. I'm in Ipswich.
B: Acton. West London. Is this your fourth?
A: Third, I think. I've lost count. They all blur a bit.
B: They do. So what do you do?
A: Senior care assistant. Residential home, forty beds. I run the floor on my shifts, do the medication rounds, write up the care notes.
B: Oh, the medication rounds. Okay, that's actually relevant to me. I'm doing a PhD on medication adherence in older people, older migrants specifically, with type 2 diabetes. And before that I was a community pharmacist.
A: Right. So you'd have done our blister packs, probably, or someone like you.
B: Probably. Can I ask you something properly? In a home, what's the main reason people don't take them? Is it refusal, or is it more that they forget?
A: In a home they don't forget, because we're stood there with the pot. It's refusal mostly. With dementia, someone'll take it fine on Monday and on Tuesday you're poisoning them. You just go back in ten minutes and try again, different face sometimes. And you write it all down, every refusal.
B: Does the different face work?
A: Often, yeh. To be fair, half of it's who's giving it them. If they trust you they'll take it.
B: That's basically my second chapter. Trust in whoever's explaining it. People assume it's a knowledge problem, like, give them a leaflet, and it's really not.
A: No. A leaflet's no good to a man who thinks it's 1962.
B: Exactly. Sorry, I'm interrogating you a bit.
A: It's fine. I'd rather that than talking about the weather.
B: Same, honestly. What do you think of the people writing the guidance? Do they understand homes?
A: Not really. Head office sends stuff down written by someone who's never done a night shift. And then they wonder why the paperwork's wrong. It's because there's two of you for twenty residents at three in the morning.
B: That's the staffing ratio, then, not the guidance.
A: It's both. Do you know what I mean? You can't separate them.
B: Fair. Yes, okay, that's fair.
A: Why that topic? If you don't mind me asking.
B: Partly my dad. He's diabetic and he's awful with his tablets. I used to tell patients off all day and then go home and he'd have skipped his metformin.
A: My dad had a heart scare a couple of years back. He's alright now, but he's the same, he only takes them when Mum's watching.
B: It's always when someone's watching. That's the finding, basically. I could save myself two years.
A: Ha. Do you like it, though? The PhD?
B: Mostly. I took a big pay cut. Some days I think I gambled wrong. But I wasn't going to stand behind a counter for thirty years.
A: I couldn't do a desk. I've been offered bits of the office side and I don't want it. I'd go mad. I'd like deputy manager eventually, just for the hours, but I want to stay on the floor.
B: You'd be good at it, I think. You don't waste words.
A: That's what the families say. They'd rather know straight.
